narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year class ranking, which placed you in the bottom decile of your school. This was substantially weaker than the average ranking of about 5.8 among students who were accepted, and it strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 26 was the next most important factor; it sits well below the 37-point average of accepted students and also pulled the outcome toward failing the bar.

Working in the opposite direction, your undergraduate GPA of 3.6 was the third most influential piece of information. This is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average among accepted applicants, so it helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, it was not strong enough to overcome the negative signals from your class rank and LSAT.

You should focus on improving your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT. Strengthening these two areas would most directly raise your chances of both admission and passing the bar on the first try.
